 Buffies and cormorants in the bay, late October 2026 OceanDiver 
 October 23 – 29 , 2026 . Salish Sea , Washington 
Yes, winter is dark and cold and wet as often as not. But there’s a lot of upside to the season too. The big shift happened this past week.
 The dry sunny calm weather we’ve been enjoying through September and October came to a halt last weekend. We’ve had some rain and strong winds. Overcast days are so dark in the morning we have to turn on lights. Here in the islands we tend to get less socked in than the rest of western Washington, so we do regularly get sunny days, which are especially nice for walking, watching wildlife, photography, and the occasional yard work. 
 But even on dark cloudy wet days, there’s good reason to go out walking. The winter birds have been arriving home for the season. Ducks and other aquatic birds fill the bays in winter, a lively change from the empty waters of summer. Last Friday we had out first wet weather in months, and coincidentally or not, that was the day the buffleheads arrived in my local bay. A few FOS Red-breasted mergansers were paddling around too. All were about 250 yards offshore, resting quietly.
 Two flocks of ducks on a rainy day: mergansers on left, buffies on right OceanDiver 
 The following day we had gale force winds out of the southeast so that bay was like a wind tunnel and the water very choppy. No ducks there. But over on the other side of the peninsula in the lee of the wind there was quite a bit of activity. Our local weather pattern is to have either wind OR rain, so in these windy conditions the sun was out for a while, making visibility much nicer. Here in the rainshadow of the Olympic mountains we get these kind of days frequently over the winter, unlike downsound (eg. Seattle) where wet grey systems settle in for weeks or months and can be kinda gloomy.
 Flock of buffleheads. The floating platform behind them is regularly brought in to anchor here every winter since this is a very protected bay. Cormorants roost on it. OceanDiver 
 Some of the buffies were feeling feisty OceanDiver 
 Drake buffie iridescence in the sunlight OceanDiver 
 Hen buffies resting OceanDiver 
 Also in the bay that day were about 40 Double-crested cormorants, many of them juveniles. A dozen were feeding on a school of baitfish by the headland. A flock of Bonapartes gulls were taking advantage of the frenzy of little fish the cormorants had stirred up. There have been more Bonapartes around near shore this winter than usual, bonus. They are one of my favorite gulls, and like the ducks, only present in our waters in winter.
 Bonapartes plunge diving OceanDiver 
 Bonapartes and cormorants feeding on baitfish OceanDiver 
 Cool how cormorants will toss a fish up in the air and swallow it on the way down OceanDiver 
 Since that day the weather has been showery off and on, with poor visibility. But I did see a flock of Red-breasted mergansers closer to shore once, fishing, and some gulls had zeroed in on their activity.
 The lighting is terrible on these next few pics, backlit, not to mention a long ways off. But it’s remarkable to me how varied in size gulls are. Our default gulls around here are the Glaucous-winged/Olympics and I forget how small the other gulls are compared to them. Mews (Short-bills) are small but Bonapartes are even smaller.
 This is just the start of the RB mergansers for the winter OceanDiver 
 Lower left: Bonapartes and GW/Olympic gull OceanDiver 
 Mew gulls are small, but look huge compared to the Bonapartes OceanDiver 
 The Bonapartes have been a bonus. But the biggest pleasure this week for me has been the return of the buffies. Right on time. Every day there’s a few more. It’s windy and rough more often than not out on the water, and the days are getting dark, but in winter, the saltchuck where these diving ducks go. Thankfully many call my local bays home for this half of the year.
 Flock of 25-30 buffies in rough seas yesterday. OceanDiver 
 💦
Current temps in the Pacific Northwest islands are in the low 50s, nights are in the low 40s. Breezy conditions. It’s been very dry this year for October but we’ve started getting some rainfall in the past few days, with more showers forecast. 
 What’s up in weather and nature in your neighborhood lately?
